about: Geotechnics (CIVE40009) is a 5-ECTS core Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Civil Engineering, running in the autumn and spring terms. Its description covers the fundamentals of soil mechanics and geotechnical engineering: how soils form, what they are made of, and how they are classified and their state assessed. It also covers one-dimensional water flow, the purpose and basic design of foundations and retaining walls, and the geological maps used in desk studies, all aimed at recognising ground hazards and planning site investigations. The programme specification gives no assessment split for this module; across the whole of Year 1 it gives 32% coursework and 68% examination. The topic list below was built from the module description.
topics: Soil origin, composition and clay minerals
Stresses in the ground and effective stress
One-dimensional flow of water through soil

notes.h: Where soils come from and what they are made of
notes.body:
In geotechnics, soil is an accumulation of mineral particles (sometimes with organic matter) that are uncemented or only weakly bonded, with the voids between them filled by water, air or both. Rock is the strongly bonded material from which soil is ultimately derived. The engineer cares about soil because its strength, stiffness and permeability all depend on how the particles are arranged and on what is in the voids.

How soils form
- Physical weathering (freeze–thaw, thermal cycling, abrasion) breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing the minerals much. It produces gravels, sands and silts, often rich in quartz.
- Chemical weathering (hydrolysis, oxidation, solution) changes the minerals themselves. Feldspars, for example, weather to clay minerals such as kaolinite. Clay-sized particles are therefore usually different minerals from the parent rock.

Residual and transported soils
- Residual soils stay where they formed, above their parent rock. They are common in warm, wet climates.
- Transported soils have been moved and deposited, and the transport process controls their character:
- Alluvial (river) deposits are sorted and layered, with sand and gravel lenses in finer material.
- Glacial till ("boulder clay") was deposited directly by ice. It is unsorted, with a very wide range of particle sizes.
- Glaciofluvial deposits were laid down by meltwater. They are sorted sands and gravels.
- Aeolian (wind-blown) deposits such as loess are very uniform silts.
- Marine deposits include the stiff, overconsolidated London Clay Formation, laid down in the Eocene.
- Colluvium is material that has moved downslope; peat is organic.

Particle sizes
BS EN ISO 14688-1 uses these boundaries: clay < 0.002 mm; silt 0.002–0.063 mm; sand 0.063–2 mm; gravel 2–63 mm; cobbles 63–200 mm; boulders > 200 mm. Coarse soils (sand and gravel) behave according to their grading and how densely they are packed. Fine soils (silt and clay) behave according to their mineralogy and water content.

Clay minerals
Clay minerals are layered silicates built from sheets of silica tetrahedra and alumina (or magnesia) octahedra. The particles are plate-shaped and carry a net negative surface charge, so they attract water molecules and cations. This adsorbed "double layer" is why clays are plastic, have very low permeability and can swell and shrink.
- Kaolinite is a 1:1 mineral (one tetrahedral sheet to one octahedral sheet). Its layers are strongly hydrogen-bonded, so it has a small specific surface and low activity.
- Illite is a 2:1 mineral whose layers are held together by potassium ions. Its properties are intermediate.
- Montmorillonite (a smectite) is a 2:1 mineral with weak bonds between layers. Water can enter between the layers, so it has a very large specific surface, high plasticity and large swelling potential.

Activity
Skempton's activity is A = IP / (percentage of particles finer than 0.002 mm). As a rough guide, A < 0.75 is inactive, 0.75–1.25 is normal and > 1.25 is active. Kaolinite is typically about 0.4, illite about 0.9, and montmorillonites well above 1. Highly active clays shrink and swell the most.

Description versus classification
Engineers first describe soil in the field (for example "firm brown slightly sandy CLAY") following BS 5930 and BS EN ISO 14688-1. They then classify it using laboratory index tests (next topic). The description records what is there; the classification groups soils that will behave in similar ways.

Exam tips: link each type of deposit to its likely engineering problems (for example, variability in till, swelling in active clays) and quote particle size boundaries exactly.

Classification puts soils into groups with similar engineering behaviour, using simple, repeatable index tests. Coarse soils are classified mainly by particle size distribution; fine soils mainly by plasticity.

Particle size distribution (PSD)
- Coarse fractions are sieved, usually washed through a 0.063 mm sieve first.
- The fine fraction is measured by sedimentation (hydrometer or pipette). This relies on Stokes' law: smaller particles settle more slowly.
- Results are plotted as percentage passing (by mass) against particle size on a log scale.
- D10, D30 and D60 are the sizes at which 10%, 30% and 60% of the soil by mass is finer. D10 is sometimes called the effective size.
- Coefficient of uniformity: Cu = D60 / D10.
- Coefficient of curvature: Cc = D30² / (D10 × D60).

A widely used criterion (from the Unified Soil Classification System) treats a sand as well graded if Cu ≥ 6 and 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3, and a gravel if Cu ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3. A uniformly graded soil has Cu close to 1, so its curve is steep. A gap-graded soil is missing a range of sizes, which shows as a flat step in the curve and usually gives Cc outside 1–3.

Worked example: D10 = 0.08 mm, D30 = 0.3 mm, D60 = 0.9 mm.
- Cu = 0.9 / 0.08 = 11.25
- Cc = 0.3² / (0.08 × 0.9) = 0.09 / 0.072 = 1.25
- The sand is well graded.

Atterberg limits (fine soils)
As water content rises, a fine soil passes from solid, to semi-solid, to plastic, to liquid.
- Liquid limit (wL): in UK practice this is usually found with the fall cone. It is the water content at which an 80 g cone with a 30° tip penetrates 20 mm in 5 s. The Casagrande cup method (25 blows) is the alternative.
- Plastic limit (wP): the water content at which a thread of soil crumbles when rolled to about 3 mm diameter.
- Plasticity index: IP = wL − wP. It is the range of water content over which the soil is plastic.
- Liquidity index: IL = (w − wP) / IP. It relates the natural water content to the limits. IL ≈ 0 means the soil is at its plastic limit (stiff); IL ≈ 1 means it is near its liquid limit (very soft). IL < 0 is typical of heavily overconsolidated clays.

Plasticity chart (BS 5930)
Plot IP against wL. The A-line, IP = 0.73(wL − 20), separates clays (above the line, symbol C) from silts (below it, symbol M). The liquid limit sets the plasticity band:
- L (low) < 35
- I (intermediate) 35–50
- H (high) 50–70
- V (very high) 70–90
- E (extremely high) > 90

Worked example: wL = 62%, wP = 26%.
- IP = 36%.
- The A-line at wL = 62 is 0.73 × 42 = 30.7.
- The point lies above the A-line with wL in the 50–70 band, so the soil is CH: clay of high plasticity.
- With w = 40%, IL = (40 − 26)/36 = 0.39.

The BS 5930 system has traditionally treated a soil with more than about 35% fines as a fine soil, whose behaviour is controlled by the fines. Laboratory tests now follow the BS EN ISO 17892 series, although some BS 1377 methods remain in use.

Exam tips: always show Cu and Cc working and the A-line value at the measured wL. State both letters of the classification (for example CH) and what they mean.

A soil element contains three phases: solids, water and air. Phase relationships link the measured masses and volumes to the quantities used in design. Draw a phase diagram every time: volumes on one side, masses (or weights) on the other.

Definitions
- Water content: w = Mw / Ms (mass of water ÷ mass of dry solids), found by oven drying at 105–110 °C.
- Specific gravity of solids: Gs = ρs / ρw. It is typically 2.6–2.8, and about 2.65 for quartz.
- Void ratio: e = Vv / Vs.
- Porosity: n = Vv / V. The two are linked by n = e/(1 + e) and e = n/(1 − n).
- Degree of saturation: Sr = Vw / Vv. It runs from 0 (dry) to 1 (saturated).
- Bulk unit weight γ = W/V; dry unit weight γd = Ws/V; γw = 9.81 kN/m³.

Key relationships (take Vs = 1)
- Sr e = w Gs. For a saturated soil this becomes e = w Gs.
- γ = (Gs + Sr e) γw / (1 + e).
- γd = Gs γw / (1 + e) = γ / (1 + w).
- γsat = (Gs + e) γw / (1 + e).
- Buoyant (submerged) unit weight: γ' = γsat − γw.

Worked example 1 (saturated clay)
w = 32%, Gs = 2.70.
- e = w Gs = 0.32 × 2.70 = 0.864
- n = 0.864 / 1.864 = 0.464
- γsat = (2.70 + 0.864) × 9.81 / 1.864 = 18.8 kN/m³
- γd = 2.70 × 9.81 / 1.864 = 14.2 kN/m³

Worked example 2 (from a tube sample)
A sample of volume 1000 cm³ has mass 1.95 kg, which falls to 1.62 kg after oven drying. Gs = 2.68.
- w = 0.33 / 1.62 = 20.4%
- γ = 1.95 × 9.81 / 0.001 = 19.1 kN/m³ (working in kN)
- γd = 15.9 kN/m³
- Vs = 1.62 / 2680 = 6.04 × 10⁻⁴ m³, so e = (1.0 − 0.604) / 0.604 = 0.654
- Sr = w Gs / e = 0.204 × 2.68 / 0.654 = 0.83

The soil is unsaturated (Sr < 1).

Describing state
For coarse soils, the density index (relative density) is ID = (emax − e) / (emax − emin). Here emax and emin are the loosest and densest void ratios found in standard tests. Loose sands (low ID) contract when sheared and may liquefy if saturated and shaken quickly. Dense sands dilate.

For fine soils, state is described by the liquidity index and by consistency terms such as soft, firm and stiff. The stress history matters too:
- A normally consolidated clay has never carried a greater vertical effective stress than it does now.
- An overconsolidated clay has been more heavily loaded in the past, for example by later-eroded overburden or by ice. London Clay is heavily overconsolidated.

Common errors
- Forgetting that w is divided by the dry mass, not the total mass.
- Mixing up e and n.
- Using γ instead of γ' below the water table when working out effective stress.

Exam tips: write the definitions first, set Vs = 1 and keep units consistent (kN, m³). Check the answer is sensible: Sr ≤ 1, and unit weights of about 16–22 kN/m³ for most natural soils.

notes.h: Stresses in the ground and effective stress
notes.body:
Terzaghi's principle of effective stress is the single most important idea in soil mechanics. Load in a saturated soil is shared between the soil skeleton (the grains in contact) and the pore water. Only the part carried by the skeleton controls strength and volume change.

The principle
- σ' = σ − u
- σ is the total stress, u is the pore water pressure and σ' is the effective stress.
- Shear strength depends on effective stress. In drained terms, τf = c' + σ' tan φ'.
- Compression and settlement are also driven by changes in effective stress, not total stress.

Total vertical stress
For layered ground with a level surface, σv = Σ γi zi: add the unit weight × thickness of each layer above the point. Use the bulk unit weight above the water table and the saturated unit weight below it. Any surface surcharge is added on top.

Pore water pressure
With a static water table, u = γw zw, where zw is the depth below the water table. Above the water table, capillary suction can make u negative in fine soils; it is often taken as zero for simplicity. If water is flowing, u is not hydrostatic (see the next topic).

Worked example
3 m of sand (γ = 17 kN/m³) lies above the water table, then 5 m of saturated sand (γsat = 20 kN/m³). At 8 m depth:
- σv = 3 × 17 + 5 × 20 = 151 kPa
- u = 5 × 9.81 = 49.1 kPa
- σ'v = 151 − 49.1 = 102 kPa

Using buoyant unit weight gives the same answer: 3 × 17 + 5 × (20 − 9.81) = 102 kPa. Two common errors:
- Measuring u from the ground surface: 8 × 9.81 = 78.5 kPa, giving 72.5 kPa.
- Using γ' and then subtracting u again (double-counting the water), giving 52.9 kPa.

Changing water levels
- Lowering the water table (for example by pumping or dewatering) reduces u and increases σ'. This can cause settlement of soft clays around an excavation.
- Raising the water table reduces σ' and so reduces frictional strength. This is one reason slopes often fail after prolonged rain.
- Excavation reduces total stress. In a clay the pore pressure falls at first (undrained unloading), then the clay slowly swells as pore pressures recover.

Horizontal stress
Effective stresses are not the same in all directions. σ'h = K0 σ'v, where K0 is the coefficient of earth pressure at rest. For a normally consolidated soil, Jaky's approximation K0 ≈ 1 − sin φ' is widely used. Overconsolidated clays can have K0 greater than 1 near the surface. Note that total horizontal stress is σh = σ'h + u: the pore pressure acts equally in all directions, but the effective stress does not.

Short-term and long-term behaviour
- Coarse soils drain quickly, so analyses use effective stresses and drained parameters (c', φ').
- Clays loaded quickly behave undrained. Their short-term strength is described by the undrained shear strength cu, a total-stress parameter.
- Over time, excess pore pressures dissipate (consolidation) and the long-term drained condition governs.

Exam tips: tabulate depth, σ, u and σ' at every layer boundary and at the water table. Sketch the profiles: they are straight lines between boundaries, with a change of slope where the unit weight changes.

notes.h: One-dimensional flow of water through soil
notes.body:
Water flows through the connected voids of a soil from points of high total head to points of low total head. Seepage matters for groundwater control in excavations, for leakage under dams, and because flowing water changes effective stresses.

Head
- Total head: h = z + u/γw. Here z is the elevation head above a chosen datum and u/γw is the pressure head. Velocity head is negligible in soils.
- Only differences in total head drive flow. The datum can be chosen anywhere, as long as it is used consistently.
- Hydraulic gradient: i = Δh / L, the head lost per unit length of flow path.

Darcy's law
- v = k i and q = k i A.
- v is the discharge (superficial) velocity, q is the flow rate and A is the gross cross-sectional area.
- k is the coefficient of permeability (hydraulic conductivity) in m/s.
- The average velocity of water through the pores (seepage velocity) is higher: vs = v/n.
- Darcy's law holds for laminar flow, which covers almost all soils except very coarse gravels.

Typical permeabilities (order of magnitude only)
- Clean gravel: above about 10⁻² m/s
- Clean sands: about 10⁻² to 10⁻⁵ m/s
- Silts: about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁸ m/s
- Intact clays: below about 10⁻⁹ m/s

Fissures and sand partings can raise the field permeability of a clay well above laboratory values.

Laboratory tests
- Constant head test (coarse soils): k = q L / (A Δh).
- Falling head test (fine soils): k = (a L / (A t)) ln(h1/h2). Here a is the area of the standpipe, A the area of the sample, and h1 and h2 the heads at the start and end of time t. Note that this is the natural logarithm.

Worked example (constant head)
A sample of length 150 mm and diameter 100 mm is under a head difference of 400 mm. It passes 520 mL of water in 120 s.
- A = π × 0.05² = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m²
- i = 0.4/0.15 = 2.67
- q = 520 × 10⁻⁶ / 120 = 4.33 × 10⁻⁶ m³/s
- k = q/(iA) = 2.07 × 10⁻⁴ m/s, which is typical of a clean sand

Layered soils
- Flow parallel to the layers: kh = Σ ki Hi / ΣHi. The most permeable layer dominates.
- Flow across the layers: kv = ΣHi / Σ(Hi/ki). The least permeable layer dominates.
- So layered deposits usually have kh much greater than kv.

Seepage and effective stress
Flowing water drags on the soil skeleton. The seepage force per unit volume is j = i γw, acting in the direction of flow.
- Downward flow increases effective stress.
- Upward flow reduces it. At depth z, σ'v = z(γ' − i γw).
- When σ'v reaches zero, a cohesionless soil loses all its strength. This is a "quick" condition (boiling or heave).
- It occurs at the critical hydraulic gradient: ic = γ'/γw = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e). This is close to 1 for most soils. For example, Gs = 2.65 and e = 0.65 give ic = 1.65/1.65 = 1.0.
- Designers keep exit gradients well below ic, for example at the base of a sheet-piled excavation, by deepening the cut-off, adding weight (a filter berm) or relieving pressure with wells.

Exam tips: define the datum and tabulate elevation, pressure and total head at each point. In falling head questions use ln, not log10, and keep a (standpipe) distinct from A (sample).

notes.h: Foundations: purpose and basic design principles
notes.body:
A foundation transfers the loads from a structure into the ground. It must do two things:
- Avoid an ultimate limit state: the ground beneath must not fail in shear (bearing failure), and the foundation must not slide or overturn.
- Avoid a serviceability limit state: total and differential settlements must not damage the structure or stop it working.

Differential settlement is usually more damaging than uniform settlement, because it distorts the frame and cracks finishes.

Types of foundation
- Shallow foundations spread load near the surface. Pads sit under columns, strips under walls, and rafts cover the whole footprint (useful on weak or variable ground, or where pads would nearly touch). As a rough guide, shallow foundations are no deeper than they are wide.
- Deep foundations (piles) carry load down to stronger strata. Piles resist load by shaft friction along their sides and end bearing at the toe. They are used where good ground is deep, loads are high, or settlement must be small.
- The choice depends on the ground profile, the loads, the groundwater, nearby structures, cost and buildability. The ground investigation is what makes that choice possible.

Bearing capacity: the idea
When a footing is loaded to failure, a wedge of soil under it pushes the soil either side sideways and upwards. Terzaghi's general expression for a strip footing is:
- qult = c Nc + q Nq + ½ γ B Nγ
- q is the overburden pressure at founding level and B is the footing width.
- The bearing capacity factors Nc, Nq and Nγ depend on the angle of shearing resistance.

Undrained clay (short term)
For a strip footing, Nc = π + 2 = 5.14, so qult = 5.14 cu + q, where q is the total overburden pressure at founding level. For a square or circular footing, a shape factor of about 1.2 is applied to the cu term. This is also the form given in Annex D of BS EN 1997-1.

Worked example
A strip footing 2 m wide sits at 1 m depth in clay with cu = 60 kPa and γ = 19 kN/m³.
- q = 19 kPa
- qult = 5.14 × 60 + 19 = 327 kPa
- That is about 655 kN per metre run

Design to Eurocode 7 (UK practice)
BS EN 1997-1 with the UK National Annex uses Design Approach 1. Two combinations are checked:
- Combination 1 (A1 + M1 + R1): permanent actions × 1.35 and variable actions × 1.5, with soil strengths unfactored. This usually governs structural design.
- Combination 2 (A2 + M2 + R1): permanent actions × 1.0 and variable actions × 1.3, with soil strengths divided by material factors (1.4 on cu, 1.25 on tan φ' and on c'). This usually governs geotechnical sizing.
- The design is acceptable if the design effect of actions does not exceed the design resistance (Ed ≤ Rd) in both combinations.
- This replaces the older "global factor of safety" approach, in which the ultimate bearing capacity was often divided by about 3 to give an allowable pressure.

These are the rules of the first-generation code, BS EN 1997-1:2004 with its UK National Annex. BSI published the second-generation BS EN 1997-1:2024 in September 2024, but the first-generation Eurocodes remain the applicable UK standards until BSI withdraws them on 30 March 2028. The second generation reorganises the partial factor approach, so check which version your module uses.

Settlement
- Immediate settlement happens as the load is applied (elastic distortion).
- Consolidation settlement happens over time in clays as excess pore pressures dissipate.
- Secondary compression (creep) can follow, especially in organic soils.
- Stress increase spreads with depth. Elastic (Boussinesq) solutions show the vertical stress under the centre falls to about 20% of the applied pressure at roughly 1.5B below a square pad and roughly 3B below a long strip. That is why the investigation must reach well below founding level.

Exam tips: always state which limit state you are checking, show the partial factors you use, and give units per metre run for strips.

Retaining walls hold back soil where the ground level changes abruptly: road cuttings, basements, quay walls and embankments.

Types of wall
- Gravity walls (mass concrete, masonry, gabions) resist the soil thrust mainly through their own weight.
- Cantilever walls are reinforced concrete L- or T-shaped walls. The soil sitting on the heel adds to the stabilising weight.
- Embedded walls (steel sheet piles, contiguous or secant bored piles, diaphragm walls) gain stability from the passive resistance of the soil in front of the embedded length, plus any props or anchors. They are used for basements and deep excavations.
- Reinforced soil walls use layers of strips or geogrids to make the soil itself into a gravity mass.

Earth pressure states
- At rest (K0): the wall does not move, for example a stiff, propped basement wall.
- Active (Ka): the wall moves away from the soil. Horizontal stress falls to a minimum as the soil mobilises its strength, and only a small movement is needed.
- Passive (Kp): the wall is pushed into the soil. Horizontal stress rises to a maximum, and a much larger movement is needed to mobilise it fully.

Rankine theory (vertical smooth wall, level backfill, drained cohesionless soil)
- Ka = (1 − sin φ')/(1 + sin φ') = tan²(45° − φ'/2)
- Kp = 1/Ka = tan²(45° + φ'/2)
- For φ' = 30°: Ka = 1/3 and Kp = 3.
- Active pressure at depth z: σ'a = Ka σ'v.
- Total active thrust from dry backfill of height H: Pa = ½ Ka γ H². It acts at H/3 above the base.

Water matters
Below the water table, the soil pressure uses effective stress (with γ'), and the full water pressure γw zw is added on top, because K = 1 for water. Water pressure can easily exceed the soil thrust. That is why walls have drainage (granular backfill, weep holes or drains) and why blocked drains are a common cause of failure.

Clays in the short term (undrained, total stress)
- σa = σv − 2cu
- Near the surface this is negative. Tension cracks can open to a depth z0 = 2cu/γ, and they may fill with water, adding hydrostatic pressure.
- Passive: σp = σv + 2cu.

Stability checks for a gravity or cantilever wall
- Sliding: base friction (plus any passive resistance relied on) must exceed the horizontal thrust.
- Overturning about the toe: the stabilising moment must exceed the overturning moment.
- Bearing: the resultant should lie within the middle third of the base, so the whole base stays in compression. The maximum toe pressure must not exceed the bearing resistance.
- Overall stability: a deep slip surface passing beneath the whole wall.

Under Eurocode 7 these are checked with partial factors, not the traditional lumped factors of safety. The traditional factors are still useful for building intuition.

Worked example
A 6 m high mass concrete wall, 3 m wide (γc = 24 kN/m³), retains dry sand with γ = 18 kN/m³ and φ' = 30°.
- Ka = 1/3, so Pa = ½ × ⅓ × 18 × 6² = 108 kN/m, acting 2 m above the base.
- Wall weight W = 24 × 6 × 3 = 432 kN/m, acting 1.5 m from the toe.
- Overturning: 648/216 = 3.0.
- Sliding with base friction angle 20°: 432 tan 20°/108 = 1.46.
- The resultant acts (648 − 216)/432 = 1.0 m from the toe. This is exactly at the edge of the middle third (eccentricity e = B/6 = 0.5 m), so the heel pressure just reaches zero and the toe pressure is 288 kPa.

Exam tips: draw the pressure diagram, split it into rectangles and triangles, and tabulate each force and its lever arm. Never forget the water.

notes.h: Rocks, geological maps and desk studies
notes.body:
Engineers need enough geology to predict what lies beneath a site before anyone drills a hole. A desk study, built largely around geological maps, is the first step of every ground investigation.

Rock types
- Igneous rocks formed by cooling magma. Examples are granite (intrusive, coarse-grained) and basalt (extrusive, fine-grained). They are usually strong and massive, but they can be jointed or deeply weathered.
- Sedimentary rocks formed from deposited and lithified sediments: sandstone, mudstone, limestone and chalk. They are layered (bedded). Strength varies widely, and some (chalk, limestone) dissolve, which forms cavities.
- Metamorphic rocks are altered by heat and pressure: slate, schist, marble. They often have a planar fabric (cleavage or foliation) that makes them weaker in one direction.

Reading a geological map
- UK maps from the British Geological Survey (BGS) show bedrock and superficial deposits. Superficial deposits are the young, mostly Quaternary soils such as alluvium, river terrace gravels and till. They may be shown on separate sheets or overlaid.
- The key gives the age order of the units. By the law of superposition, in undisturbed strata the younger beds lie on top of the older ones.
- Strike is the direction of a horizontal line on a bedding plane. Dip is the maximum slope of the plane, measured at right angles to the strike.

Outcrop patterns
- Horizontal beds follow the topographic contours.
- Vertical beds run straight across the topography, whatever the relief.
- Dipping beds form a V where they cross valleys. Beds dipping upstream V upstream. Beds dipping downstream more steeply than the valley floor V downstream.
- Folds: in an eroded anticline the oldest beds are in the core; in a syncline the youngest are.
- Faults offset the beds. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down (extension). In a reverse or thrust fault it moves up (compression). Faults can bring very different materials side by side and may carry water.
- An unconformity is a buried erosion surface, so younger beds rest on older, often tilted, rocks.

Calculations
- Apparent dip on a section line at angle β to the strike: tan α = tan δ sin β, where δ is the true dip.
- True thickness from an outcrop width w measured perpendicular to strike on flat ground: t = w sin δ.
- Example: a true dip of 30° seen on a section at 40° to the strike gives an apparent dip of arctan(0.577 × 0.643) = 20.4°.

Cross-sections
Draw the topographic profile along the section line. Mark where each boundary crosses the line, then project the boundaries down using the apparent dip for that line. Boreholes shown on the section must agree with the map.

The desk study
Its purpose is to build an initial ground model and a list of hazards before money is spent on fieldwork. Typical sources:
- BGS geological maps, memoirs and borehole records
- Historical Ordnance Survey maps, which show former quarries, ponds, filled ground and old industrial uses
- Coal mining reports (from the Mining Remediation Authority, as the Coal Authority has been called since November 2024, in coalfield areas)
- Flood and groundwater information
- Aerial photographs and satellite imagery
- Records of utilities and existing structures
- Previous site investigation reports

A site walkover then checks the desk study on the ground. It looks for things like seepage, hummocky ground that may indicate landslipping, cracked buildings and leaning trees.

Exam tips: in map questions, identify the oldest and youngest units first, then work out the structure (dip, folds, faults, unconformities) before drawing the section. Always say where a borehole would confirm your interpretation.

Unforeseen ground conditions are a common cause of delay, extra cost and failure on civil engineering projects. The purpose of site investigation is to reduce that risk to an acceptable level by finding out what the ground is like before design and construction. In the UK the main guidance is BS 5930 (code of practice for ground investigations), used with BS EN 1997-2 and the BS EN ISO standards for field and laboratory testing.

Common geotechnical hazards (UK examples)
- Shrinkable clays: high-plasticity clays such as London Clay shrink and swell with seasonal moisture change. Trees make this worse by drying the clay, which can cause subsidence and heave of shallow foundations.
- Soft and compressible soils such as alluvium and peat give large, slow settlements.
- Dissolution features: chalk and limestone can contain solution pipes and cavities, giving sudden collapse (sinkholes).
- Mining: old shallow workings and unrecorded mine shafts in coalfields.
- Made ground and contamination: variable fill, voids, buried obstructions and polluted ground on former industrial sites.
- Slope instability: landslides, which are often reactivated on old slip surfaces in clays.
- Groundwater: high or artesian water, flooding, and seepage into excavations.
- Loose saturated sands, which can liquefy under strong shaking. This is mainly a concern in seismic regions.
- Aggressive ground: sulfates that attack buried concrete.

Stages of an investigation
- Desk study and site walkover: a preliminary ground model and hazard list.
- Preliminary investigation: a few boreholes or trial pits to confirm the geology and refine the design options.
- Main (design) investigation: enough data to design the chosen scheme.
- Supplementary or construction-stage investigation and monitoring, where needed.

Field methods
- Trial pits, dug by machine: cheap, and they show the soil fabric and groundwater seepage, but they are shallow (a few metres).
- Cable percussion boreholes (common in UK soils): give samples and allow in-situ tests at depth.
- Rotary coring: for rock and very stiff ground, recovering continuous core.
- Standard Penetration Test (SPT): a 63.5 kg hammer falls 760 mm to drive a split-barrel sampler. After a 150 mm seating drive, N is the number of blows for the next 300 mm. It is mainly used in sands and gravels to judge density.
- Cone Penetration Test (CPT): a 60° cone, typically of 10 cm² base area, is pushed at a steady 20 mm/s. It gives a continuous record of cone resistance and sleeve friction (plus pore pressure in CPTU). It is excellent for profiling soft soils, but it recovers no sample.
- Sampling: thin-walled tube samples of fine soils for strength and consolidation tests, and bulk or disturbed samples for classification.
- Groundwater: record water strikes while drilling, and install standpipes or piezometers for longer-term monitoring.

Laboratory testing
- Classification: water content, Atterberg limits, particle size distribution.
- Strength: triaxial tests, shear box.
- Compressibility: oedometer.
- Permeability.
- Chemical tests: sulfate, pH, contaminants.

Planning the investigation
- Spacing and depth of exploratory holes depend on the structure, the variability of the ground and the hazards identified.
- Holes must go deep enough to cover the ground that will be significantly stressed by the foundations (see the stress bulb in the foundations topic), and deeper if weak layers or mining are suspected.
- The results go into a factual report, then an interpretative report and ground model. Hazards and their mitigation are tracked in a geotechnical risk register.

Exam tips: in essay questions, move from desk study, to hazards, to targeted fieldwork, to testing, to ground model. Justify every hole and test by the hazard or design parameter it addresses.

cards.b: Physical weathering breaks rock into fragments of the same minerals (gravel, sand, silt). Chemical weathering alters the minerals, for example feldspar to clay minerals, producing clay-sized particles.
Clay < 0.002 mm; silt 0.002–0.063 mm; sand 0.063–2 mm; gravel 2–63 mm; cobbles 63–200 mm; boulders > 200 mm.
Soil deposited directly by ice: unsorted, with a very wide range of particle sizes from clay to boulders, so it is often highly variable. Sometimes called boulder clay.

Kaolinite: 1:1 layers, strongly hydrogen-bonded, low specific surface and activity. Montmorillonite: 2:1 layers, weakly bonded so water enters between them; very high specific surface, plasticity and swelling.
A = plasticity index / percentage of clay-sized particles (< 0.002 mm). Roughly: inactive < 0.75, normal 0.75–1.25, active > 1.25.
Plate-shaped clay particles carry a negative surface charge and hold a layer of adsorbed water and cations. This lets them deform without cracking over a range of water contents.
Soil that has formed in place by weathering of the rock beneath it and has not been transported. Common in warm, humid climates.
Cu = D60/D10. Cu near 1 means uniformly graded; large Cu means a wide range of sizes.
Cc = D30²/(D10 × D60). For a well-graded soil, 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3 (USCS criterion, together with Cu ≥ 6 for sands or ≥ 4 for gravels).
Water content at which an 80 g, 30° cone penetrates 20 mm into the soil in 5 s (UK standard method).
Water content at which a thread of soil just crumbles when rolled to about 3 mm diameter.
IP = wL − wP. IL = (w − wP)/IP: IL ≈ 0 means at the plastic limit; IL ≈ 1 means near the liquid limit.
IP = 0.73(wL − 20). Points above the line are clays (C); points below are silts (M).
Liquid limit: low < 35, intermediate 35–50, high 50–70, very high 70–90, extremely high > 90.
e = Vv/Vs; n = Vv/V. n = e/(1 + e); e = n/(1 − n).
w = mass of water ÷ mass of dry solids (not total mass). Measured by oven drying at 105–110 °C.
Links saturation, void ratio, water content and specific gravity. For a saturated soil (Sr = 1): e = w Gs.
γd = Gs γw/(1 + e) = γ/(1 + w).
γ' = γsat − γw. Used to calculate effective stress below a static water table.
ID = (emax − e)/(emax − emin). Describes how loose or dense a coarse soil is relative to its loosest and densest states.
A clay whose current vertical effective stress is lower than the maximum it has carried in the past (for example, because overburden was eroded). London Clay is heavily overconsolidated.
σ' = σ − u. Effective stress (carried by the soil skeleton) controls shear strength and volume change in saturated soils.
u = γw zw, where zw is the depth below the water table and γw = 9.81 kN/m³.

cards.f: Total vertical stress in layered ground
cards.b: σv = Σ γi zi (bulk unit weight above the water table, saturated below), plus any surface surcharge.
Coefficient of earth pressure at rest: σ'h/σ'v with no lateral strain. Normally consolidated: K0 ≈ 1 − sin φ' (Jaky). Can exceed 1 in heavily overconsolidated clay.

cards.f: Effect of lowering the water table
cards.b: Pore pressure falls and effective stress rises, so the soil compresses. This can cause settlement of nearby soft clays during dewatering.
τf = c' + σ' tan φ', where σ' is the effective normal stress on the failure plane.
Total-stress strength of a saturated clay loaded too quickly for pore pressures to dissipate. Used for short-term (end-of-construction) analyses.
h = z + u/γw (elevation head + pressure head). Water flows from high to low total head; velocity head is negligible in soils.
v = k i and q = k i A, where i = Δh/L. Valid for laminar flow. Seepage velocity through the pores is v/n.
Used for coarse soils: k = qL/(A Δh).
Used for fine soils: k = (aL/(At)) ln(h1/h2), with a = standpipe area and A = sample area.
ic = γ'/γw = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e), typically about 1. Upward flow at this gradient makes σ' = 0 (quick condition) in a cohesionless soil.
j = i γw per unit volume, acting in the direction of flow. Upward seepage reduces effective stress; downward seepage increases it.
Parallel to layers: kh = Σki Hi/ΣHi. Across layers: kv = ΣHi/Σ(Hi/ki). Usually kh ≫ kv.
ULS: bearing (shear) failure, sliding or overturning: the ground or foundation fails. SLS: settlement or movement that impairs use or appearance of the structure.

cards.f: Undrained bearing capacity of a strip
cards.b: qult = (π + 2)cu + q = 5.14 cu + q, where q is total overburden pressure at founding level. Multiply the cu term by about 1.2 for square or circular footings.
qult = c Nc + q Nq + ½ γ B Nγ; the N factors depend on φ.
A1 + M1 + R1: γG = 1.35, γQ = 1.5 on actions; soil strengths unfactored.
A2 + M2 + R1: γG = 1.0, γQ = 1.3; strengths factored: γcu = 1.4, γφ' = 1.25 (on tan φ'), γc' = 1.25.
The two components of a pile's capacity: shear along the pile sides and bearing at the toe.
Time-dependent settlement of a clay as excess pore pressures dissipate and effective stress rises.
Active: wall moves away from the soil, so horizontal stress falls to a minimum (Ka). Passive: wall pushed into the soil, so stress rises to a maximum (Kp). Passive needs much larger movement.
Pa = ½ Ka γ H² per metre run, acting at H/3 above the base.
z0 = 2cu/γ, where the active total pressure σv − 2cu becomes zero. Cracks may fill with water.
If the resultant base reaction lies within the middle third of the base (eccentricity ≤ B/6), the whole base stays in compression.
A wall (sheet piles, bored piles, diaphragm wall) that relies on passive resistance below excavation level, often with props or anchors.
Water pressure acts with K = 1 on the full submerged height and can exceed the soil thrust. Drains and weep holes stop it building up.
Strike: direction of a horizontal line on a bedding plane. Dip: maximum inclination of the plane, measured perpendicular to the strike.
tan α = tan δ sin β, where δ is the true dip and β is the angle between the section line and the strike. Apparent dip is always ≤ true dip.
Anticline: oldest beds exposed in the core, beds dip away from the axis. Syncline: youngest beds in the core, beds dip towards the axis.
Normal: hanging wall moves down relative to footwall (extension). Reverse/thrust: hanging wall moves up (compression).
Young, mostly Quaternary, unconsolidated deposits (alluvium, river terrace deposits, till, head) lying on bedrock; shown separately on BGS maps.

cards.b: Horizontal beds follow the contours, so their outcrop forms a V pointing upstream in a valley.
To build a preliminary ground model and identify hazards (geology, groundwater, mining, made ground, flooding) before planning and pricing fieldwork.

questions.q: Which clay mineral is most likely to cause large swelling and shrinkage when its water content changes?
questions.why: Montmorillonite (a smectite) has weak bonds between its 2:1 layers, so water can enter between them and the mineral swells strongly. Kaolinite's 1:1 layers are tightly hydrogen-bonded, so it swells little. Illite's layers are held together by potassium ions, so it lies between the two. Quartz is not a clay mineral: it forms bulky silt and sand grains with no adsorbed water layer.

questions.q: A clay has plasticity index IP = 45% and a clay fraction (< 0.002 mm) of 25%. What is its activity and how would it be described?
questions.why: Activity = IP / clay fraction = 45/25 = 1.8, which is above 1.25, so the clay is active. 0.56 comes from inverting the ratio (25/45). Calling 1.8 'normal' uses the wrong band, since normal activity is only about 0.75–1.25. 0.45 comes from dividing IP by 100 instead of by the clay percentage.

questions.q: Explain why a clay and a sand of the same dry density can behave very differently in engineering terms. Refer to particle size, mineralogy and the role of water.
markScheme: Clay particles are < 0.002 mm and plate-shaped; sand grains are 0.063–2 mm and bulky (often quartz)
Clay minerals carry a negative surface charge and adsorbed water, giving plasticity and cohesion-like behaviour; sand has no such effects
Clay has a far larger specific surface, so water content strongly changes its consistency (Atterberg limits); sand's behaviour is controlled by packing and grading
Clay permeability is many orders of magnitude lower, so clays respond undrained in the short term and consolidate slowly; sands drain almost at once
Active clays shrink and swell with moisture change; sands do not
questions.modelAnswer: Sand grains are bulky particles between 0.063 and 2 mm, usually quartz, and they interact only through contact friction. Their behaviour depends on how densely they are packed and how well graded they are. Clay particles are smaller than 0.002 mm, plate-shaped clay minerals with a negative surface charge. They hold a layer of adsorbed water and cations. Because their specific surface is enormous, the amount of water present changes their consistency: the same clay can be hard, plastic or almost liquid depending on its water content, which is what the Atterberg limits measure. Clays have very low permeability (often below about 10⁻⁹ m/s, compared with roughly 10⁻²–10⁻⁵ m/s for clean sands). So when a clay is loaded quickly, pore pressures cannot dissipate: it behaves undrained in the short term and settles slowly by consolidation. A sand drains almost immediately. Active clays such as smectite-rich soils also shrink and swell as their water content changes, which sands do not.

questions.q: A fine soil has liquid limit 62% and plastic limit 26%. How is it classified on the BS 5930 plasticity chart?
options: CV – clay of very high plasticity
questions.why: IP = 62 − 26 = 36. The A-line at wL = 62 is 0.73 × (62 − 20) = 30.7, so the point plots above the line and the soil is a clay. A liquid limit of 62 lies in the 50–70 band, so it is high plasticity: CH. CV would need wL between 70 and 90. MH would need the point to plot below the A-line. CI would need wL between 35 and 50.

questions.q: A sand has D10 = 0.08 mm, D30 = 0.3 mm and D60 = 0.9 mm. Which description fits its grading?
options: Uniformly graded, because Cu is close to 1
Gap graded, because Cc is outside 1–3
It cannot be judged without the Atterberg limits
questions.why: Cu = 0.9/0.08 = 11.25 and Cc = 0.3²/(0.08 × 0.9) = 1.25. Cu is above 6 and Cc lies between 1 and 3, so the sand is well graded. It is not uniformly graded, because Cu is far from 1. Cc = 1.25 lies inside the 1–3 range, so the curve shows no gap. Atterberg limits describe the plasticity of fines, not the grading of a sand.

questions.q: A clay has liquid limit 62%, plastic limit 26% and natural water content 40%. Calculate the plasticity and liquidity indices, classify the soil on the plasticity chart, and comment on its likely consistency.
markScheme: A-line at wL = 62: 0.73 × 42 = 30.7; IP = 36 lies above it, so it is a clay
wL in 50–70 band, so high plasticity: CH
IL between 0 and 1: plastic state, nearer the plastic limit than the liquid limit, so a firm to stiff consistency is likely (to be confirmed by description or strength tests)
questions.modelAnswer: IP = wL − wP = 62 − 26 = 36%. IL = (w − wP)/IP = (40 − 26)/36 = 0.39. The A-line at wL = 62 gives IP = 0.73(62 − 20) = 30.7. The measured IP of 36 lies above it, so the soil is a clay, and wL = 62 falls in the high band (50–70). The classification is therefore CH, clay of high plasticity. An IL of 0.39 means the natural water content is within the plastic range and closer to the plastic limit than to the liquid limit. The clay is therefore likely to be firm rather than very soft, though consistency should be confirmed by field description or strength testing. A high-plasticity clay like this is also likely to shrink and swell noticeably with seasonal moisture change.

questions.q: A saturated clay has water content 32% and Gs = 2.70. What is its void ratio?
questions.why: For a saturated soil, e = w Gs = 0.32 × 2.70 = 0.864. 0.464 is the porosity, n = e/(1 + e), not the void ratio. 0.119 comes from dividing w by Gs instead of multiplying. 0.320 simply takes the void ratio to equal the water content, ignoring Gs.

questions.q: A soil has bulk unit weight 19.5 kN/m³ and water content 20%. What is its dry unit weight?
questions.why: γd = γ/(1 + w) = 19.5/1.20 = 16.25 kN/m³. 15.6 comes from multiplying by (1 − w), which wrongly treats w as a fraction of the total mass. 23.4 multiplies by (1 + w), which adds water instead of removing it. 17.5 subtracts w × γw from γ, which mixes a mass ratio with the unit weight of water and has no physical basis.

questions.q: A 1000 cm³ tube sample has mass 1.95 kg and an oven-dry mass of 1.62 kg. Gs = 2.68. Find the water content, bulk and dry unit weights, void ratio and degree of saturation.
markScheme: Sr = w Gs/e = 0.204 × 2.68/0.654 = 0.83, so the sample is partly saturated
questions.modelAnswer: Mass of water = 1.95 − 1.62 = 0.33 kg, so w = 0.33/1.62 = 0.204 (20.4%). Bulk unit weight γ = (1.95 × 9.81 N)/(1.0 × 10⁻³ m³) = 19.1 kN/m³. Dry unit weight γd = (1.62 × 9.81)/(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 15.9 kN/m³; check: 19.1/1.204 = 15.9 kN/m³. Volume of solids Vs = Ms/(Gs ρw) = 1.62/2680 = 6.04 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Voids volume = 1.0 × 10⁻³ − 6.04 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.96 × 10⁻⁴ m³, so e = 3.96/6.04 = 0.654. Sr = w Gs/e = 0.204 × 2.68/0.654 = 0.83. The sample is about 83% saturated.

questions.q: Ground: 3 m of sand (γ = 17 kN/m³) above the water table, over 5 m of saturated sand (γsat = 20 kN/m³). Water table at 3 m depth, hydrostatic conditions. What is the vertical effective stress at 8 m depth?
questions.why: σv = 3 × 17 + 5 × 20 = 151 kPa and u = 5 × 9.81 = 49.1 kPa, so σ'v = 102 kPa. 151 kPa is the total stress, before the pore pressure is subtracted. 72.5 kPa measures the pore pressure from the ground surface (8 m of water) instead of from the water table (5 m). 52.9 kPa uses the buoyant unit weight below the water table and then subtracts u again, so it double-counts the water.

questions.q: Which of these would increase the vertical effective stress at depth in a saturated clay layer?
options: Lowering the water table by pumping
Steady upward seepage through the layer
Excavating soil from above the layer
questions.why: Lowering the water table reduces the pore pressure at depth, so σ' = σ − u increases. Raising the water table increases u and reduces σ'. Upward seepage raises pore pressures above hydrostatic, which also reduces σ'. Excavation removes total stress, which reduces effective stress in the long term.

questions.q: The site in the worked example (3 m sand, γ = 17 kN/m³, above a 3 m-deep water table; 5 m saturated sand, γsat = 20 kN/m³) is underlain by clay with γsat = 19 kN/m³. (a) Find σ'v at 10 m depth. (b) The water table is lowered by 2 m by dewatering; assume the drained sand has γ = 17 kN/m³. Find the new σ'v at 10 m and explain the consequence for the clay.
markScheme: Increase of about 13.6 kPa in σ'v (total stress falls slightly but pore pressure falls more)
The clay will consolidate (settle) over time as excess pore pressures dissipate, because volume change is driven by effective stress
questions.modelAnswer: (a) At 10 m: σv = 3 × 17 + 5 × 20 + 2 × 19 = 189 kPa. The water table is at 3 m, so u = 7 × 9.81 = 68.7 kPa and σ'v = 189 − 68.7 = 120.3 kPa. (b) With the water table at 5 m, the top 5 m has γ = 17 kN/m³: σv = 5 × 17 + 3 × 20 + 2 × 19 = 183 kPa. u = 5 × 9.81 = 49.1 kPa, so σ'v = 183 − 49.1 = 134.0 kPa. The effective stress rises by about 13.6 kPa: total stress falls slightly because the drained sand is lighter, but pore pressure falls by much more. Because compression of the clay depends on effective stress, the clay will consolidate and the ground surface will settle. In a low-permeability clay this happens gradually as pore pressures in the clay adjust. This is why dewatering near existing buildings needs care.

questions.q: In a constant head test, a 150 mm long, 100 mm diameter sample under a 400 mm head difference passes 520 mL in 120 s. What is k?
questions.why: q = 520 × 10⁻⁶/120 = 4.33 × 10⁻⁶ m³/s, i = 0.40/0.15 = 2.67 and A = π × 0.05² = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m², so k = q/(iA) = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ m/s. 5.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s divides q by A only, leaving out the hydraulic gradient. 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s uses the 0.1 m diameter as the radius, which makes the area four times too large. 1.5 × 10⁻³ m/s inverts the gradient (L/Δh = 0.375 instead of 2.67).

questions.q: For steady upward seepage through a sand, a quick condition develops when:
questions.why: A quick condition is reached when the upward seepage force (i γw per unit volume) balances the buoyant weight γ', so σ' = 0, giving ic = γ'/γw. Setting i = γsat/γw counts the water's own weight, which buoyancy already balances, so it overestimates ic by about a factor of two. Permeability alone does not set the condition: it is the gradient that matters, although fine sands are most prone in practice. Hydrostatic pore pressure means no flow at all, so no seepage force acts.

questions.q: A falling head test is carried out on a clayey silt sample 100 mm long and 100 mm in diameter. The standpipe has an internal diameter of 5 mm. The head falls from 1.20 m to 0.60 m in 600 s. Calculate k and comment on the result.
markScheme: k = (aL/(At)) ln(h1/h2)
Comment: consistent with a silt or clayey silt; using log10 instead of ln would give 1.3 × 10⁻⁷ m/s (wrong)
questions.modelAnswer: Standpipe area a = π × (0.005/2)² = 1.96 × 10⁻⁵ m². Sample area A = π × 0.05² = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m². L = 0.10 m and t = 600 s. k = (aL/(At)) ln(h1/h2) = (1.96 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10)/(7.85 × 10⁻³ × 600) × ln(1.20/0.60) = 4.17 × 10⁻⁷ × 0.693 = 2.9 × 10⁻⁷ m/s. This lies in the range expected for silts and clayey silts, which is why a falling head test (rather than a constant head test) was appropriate: the flow would be too small to measure accurately under constant head. Using log10 by mistake would give 1.3 × 10⁻⁷ m/s.

questions.q: A strip footing 2 m wide at 1 m depth bears on clay with cu = 60 kPa and γ = 19 kN/m³. What is the short-term ultimate bearing pressure?
questions.why: qult = (π + 2)cu + q = 5.14 × 60 + 19 × 1 = 327 kPa. 308 kPa leaves out the overburden term q = 19 kPa. 389 kPa applies the 1.2 shape factor for a square or circular footing, which does not apply to a long strip. 239 kPa is the Eurocode 7 Combination 2 design value (cu divided by 1.4), not the characteristic ultimate pressure.

questions.q: In UK practice under BS EN 1997-1 Design Approach 1, which description fits Combination 2?
options: Permanent actions × 1.0, variable actions × 1.3, and soil strengths reduced by material factors
Permanent actions × 1.35, variable actions × 1.5, and soil strengths unfactored
Unfactored actions and strengths, with the bearing capacity divided by a global factor of about 3
Unfactored soil strengths, with a resistance factor of 1.4 applied to bearing resistance
questions.why: Combination 2 uses set A2 for actions (1.0 and 1.3) and set M2 for materials (for example cu ÷ 1.4), with R1 resistance factors of 1.0. Factors of 1.35 and 1.5 with unfactored strengths are Combination 1. A global factor of about 3 is the traditional allowable-pressure approach that limit state design replaced. Putting the main factor on resistance is how Design Approach 2 works, which is not the UK's choice for spread foundations.

questions.q: The 2 m wide strip footing above (cu = 60 kPa, γ = 19 kN/m³, depth 1 m) carries characteristic loads Gk = 250 kN/m and Qk = 100 kN/m (including self-weight). Check the undrained bearing resistance for DA1 Combination 2.
markScheme: Design load Ed = 1.0 × 250 + 1.3 × 100 = 380 kN/m
Design strength cu,d = 60/1.4 = 42.9 kPa
Design resistance per unit area = 5.14 × 42.9 + 19 = 239 kPa; Rd = 239 × 2 = 479 kN/m
Ed ≤ Rd (utilisation ≈ 0.79), so Combination 2 is satisfied; Combination 1 must also be checked (Ed = 487.5 kN/m vs Rd = 655 kN/m)
questions.modelAnswer: In Combination 2, actions take set A2: Ed = 1.0 × 250 + 1.3 × 100 = 380 kN/m. Material set M2 reduces the undrained strength: cu,d = 60/1.4 = 42.9 kPa. Resistance factors R1 are 1.0. Design bearing resistance per unit area = (π + 2) × 42.9 + 19 = 239 kPa, so Rd = 239 × 2 = 479 kN/m. Since 380 ≤ 479 (utilisation about 0.79), Combination 2 is satisfied. For completeness, Combination 1 gives Ed = 1.35 × 250 + 1.5 × 100 = 487.5 kN/m against Rd = 327 × 2 = 655 kN/m (utilisation about 0.74), so it is also satisfied. Settlement (SLS) would still need a separate check.

questions.q: Using Rankine theory, what is the active earth pressure coefficient for a drained sand with φ' = 30°?
questions.why: Ka = (1 − sin 30°)/(1 + sin 30°) = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333. 3.0 is the passive coefficient, Kp = 1/Ka. 0.5 is Jaky's at-rest coefficient, 1 − sin φ', which applies when the wall does not move. 0.577 is tan 30°, a friction coefficient, not an earth pressure coefficient.

questions.q: The resultant of the base reaction under a 3 m wide gravity wall acts 0.8 m from the toe. What does this imply?
options: The resultant is outside the middle third, so part of the base under the heel loses contact and the toe pressure rises sharply
The base is in uniform compression because the resultant is near the centre
The wall must be about to slide
Nothing can be said without knowing the soil's angle of shearing resistance
questions.why: The middle third of a 3 m base runs from 1.0 to 2.0 m from the toe. At 0.8 m the eccentricity is 0.7 m, more than B/6 = 0.5 m, so the heel end of the base would be in tension. Soil cannot take tension, so contact is lost there and pressure concentrates under the toe. Uniform pressure needs the resultant at the centre (1.5 m). The position of the resultant says nothing directly about sliding, which depends on the ratio of horizontal force to base friction. The middle-third check is a matter of statics and needs no soil strength parameter.

questions.q: Distinguish at-rest, active and passive earth pressure, and explain which you would use for (i) a propped basement wall and (ii) the soil in front of the embedded toe of a cantilever sheet pile wall.
markScheme: At rest (K0): no lateral strain in the soil; e.g. K0 ≈ 1 − sin φ' for normally consolidated soil
Active (Ka): wall moves away from the soil; minimum lateral pressure, mobilised by small movement
Passive (Kp): wall pushed into the soil; maximum lateral pressure, needs much larger movement
(i) Stiff propped basement wall: little movement, so pressures closer to at rest (K0) on the retained side
(ii) Soil in front of the toe: the wall is pushed into it, so passive resistance (Kp), often with a reduction or factor because full passive needs large movement
questions.modelAnswer: At-rest pressure applies when the soil undergoes no lateral strain. The ratio σ'h/σ'v is then K0, about 1 − sin φ' for a normally consolidated soil and larger for overconsolidated clay. If a wall moves away from the retained soil, the soil mobilises its shear strength and the lateral stress falls to the active minimum, Ka σ'v. Only a small movement is needed for this. If a wall is pushed into the soil, the lateral stress rises to the passive maximum, Kp σ'v, which needs a much larger movement to mobilise fully. (i) A stiff, propped basement wall barely moves, so the retained soil stays close to at rest and K0 is the appropriate basis (the props stop it reaching active). (ii) Below excavation level, the toe of a cantilever sheet pile wall is pushed forward into the soil in front, so that soil provides passive resistance. Designers do not rely on the full theoretical Kp, because the movement needed to mobilise it may be unacceptable.

questions.q: A bed has a true dip of 30°. What apparent dip will be seen on a cross-section drawn at 40° to the strike?
questions.why: tan α = tan 30° × sin 40° = 0.577 × 0.643 = 0.371, so α = 20.4°. 23.9° uses cos 40° instead of sin 40°, which is the formula for an angle measured from the dip direction rather than from the strike. 19.3° multiplies the angle itself by sin 40° (30 × 0.643) instead of working with tangents. 30° is the true dip, which is seen only on a section perpendicular to the strike.

questions.q: On an eroded, level surface across a fold, the oldest beds are found in the centre and the beds dip away from the axis on both sides. What is the structure?
questions.why: In an anticline the beds arch upwards, so erosion exposes the oldest beds in the core and the limbs dip away from the axis. A syncline has the youngest beds in the core and the limbs dip towards the axis. A normal fault displaces beds across a single plane rather than repeating them symmetrically. An unconformity is a buried erosion surface between two rock sequences, not a symmetrical fold pattern.

questions.q: A sandstone bed dipping at 25° crops out on level ground with an outcrop width of 50 m measured perpendicular to the strike. (a) Find its true thickness. (b) Describe how the outcrop of horizontal beds appears where they cross a valley, and why.
markScheme: t = w sin δ = 50 × sin 25°
Horizontal beds follow the topographic contours
So their outcrop forms a V pointing upstream in a valley, because the contours themselves V upstream
questions.modelAnswer: (a) On level ground, measured perpendicular to the strike, true thickness t = w sin δ = 50 × sin 25° = 50 × 0.423 = 21.1 m. (b) A horizontal bed is at the same elevation everywhere, so its boundaries run parallel to the topographic contours. Where a valley cuts down, the contours bend upstream, so the outcrop of horizontal beds also forms a V pointing upstream. The steeper the valley, the sharper the V.

questions.q: A house on high-plasticity clay next to a line of mature trees shows cracking that opens in late summer and partly closes in winter. What is the most likely hazard?
options: Seasonal shrinkage and swelling of the clay
Dissolution of chalk forming a sinkhole
Collapse of old coal mine workings
questions.why: High-plasticity clays lose water in summer (made worse by tree roots) and shrink, then swell again in winter, so the cracks open and close with the seasons. Dissolution sinkholes occur in chalk or limestone and usually cause sudden, one-off collapse, not seasonal movement. Liquefaction needs loose saturated sand and strong shaking. Mine workings occur in coalfield geology, and their collapse is not seasonal.

questions.q: What is the SPT N value?
options: The number of blows of a 63.5 kg hammer falling 760 mm to drive the sampler 300 mm, after a 150 mm seating drive
The number of blows needed to drive the sampler the first 150 mm
The cone resistance in MPa recorded at a steady penetration rate
The total number of blows for the full 450 mm drive
questions.why: N counts only the blows for the 300 mm after the 150 mm seating drive, which is discarded because the bottom of the borehole is disturbed. Counting the first 150 mm uses exactly the seating blows that are excluded. Cone resistance at a steady rate comes from the CPT, a different test. Counting the full 450 mm wrongly includes the seating drive.

questions.q: List the main sources of information for a desk study on a UK site and state what each would tell you.
markScheme: BGS geological maps, memoirs and borehole records: expected bedrock and superficial geology, previous borehole logs
Historical Ordnance Survey maps: former land uses, filled ponds or pits, old buildings and industry (made ground and contamination)
Coal mining reports (in coalfields): recorded workings, shafts and the risk of shallow mining
Environment Agency flood maps and groundwater information; aerial photographs or imagery: landslips, drainage, changes over time
Utility and existing-structure records and previous site investigation reports; followed by a site walkover
questions.modelAnswer: A desk study draws on several sources. BGS geological maps and memoirs show the expected bedrock and superficial deposits, and the BGS borehole records give logs from nearby holes. A run of historical Ordnance Survey maps reveals former land use: filled ponds, pits and quarries, old buildings and industrial activity. These point to made ground, obstructions and possible contamination. In coalfield areas, a coal mining report shows recorded workings and shafts. Environment Agency flood maps and groundwater information indicate flood risk and likely water levels. Aerial photographs and satellite imagery can reveal landslips, drainage paths and changes over time. Records of utilities, existing structures and earlier site investigation reports avoid repeating work and identify buried services. The findings are checked by a site walkover and used to plan the fieldwork.

questions.q: A 6 m high mass concrete gravity wall with a rectangular cross-section 3 m wide (γc = 24 kN/m³) retains level, dry sand backfill with γ = 18 kN/m³ and φ' = 30°. Treat the back of the wall as smooth and vertical. (a) Calculate Rankine's Ka and Kp. [2] (b) Find the active thrust per metre and its line of action. [3] (c) Find the factor of safety against overturning about the toe. [3] (d) Taking a base friction angle of 20° and ignoring passive resistance, find the factor of safety against sliding. [3] (e) Locate the resultant on the base, and find the toe and heel pressures. [4] (f) The drains block and the water table rises to 3 m below the top of the wall (γsat = 20 kN/m³ below it). Recalculate the total horizontal thrust and comment. [5]
markScheme: (b) Pa = ½ × ⅓ × 18 × 6² = 108 kN/m acting at H/3 = 2 m above the base
(c) W = 24 × 6 × 3 = 432 kN/m at 1.5 m from the toe; MR = 648 kNm/m; MO = 216 kNm/m; FoS = 3.0
(d) Resistance = 432 tan 20° = 157 kN/m; FoS = 157/108 = 1.46
(e) x = (648 − 216)/432 = 1.0 m from the toe; e = 0.5 m = B/6; q = (W/B)(1 ± 6e/B): toe 288 kPa, heel 0 kPa
(f) σ'a at 3 m = 18 kPa; at 6 m = ⅓(54 + 3 × 10.19) = 28.2 kPa; soil thrust = 27 + 54 + 15.3 = 96.3 kN/m; water thrust = ½ × 9.81 × 3² = 44.1 kN/m
(f) Total = 140.4 kN/m, about 30% more than the dry case, even though the soil part fell; overturning FoS falls to about 2.6 and sliding is worse
Comment: shows why drainage is essential; Eurocode 7 would check these with partial factors rather than lumped FoS
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Ka = (1 − sin 30°)/(1 + sin 30°) = 0.5/1.5 = 1/3. Kp = 1/Ka = 3.

(b) For dry backfill, σ'a = Ka γ z, which rises linearly to ⅓ × 18 × 6 = 36 kPa at the base. Pa = ½ × 36 × 6 = 108 kN/m, acting at the centroid of the triangle, H/3 = 2 m above the base.

(c) Wall weight W = 24 × 6 × 3 = 432 kN/m, acting through the centre of the base, 1.5 m from the toe. Restoring moment MR = 432 × 1.5 = 648 kNm/m. Overturning moment MO = 108 × 2 = 216 kNm/m. FoS = 648/216 = 3.0.

(d) Base sliding resistance = W tan δb = 432 × tan 20° = 432 × 0.364 = 157 kN/m. FoS = 157/108 = 1.46.

(e) Taking moments about the toe, the resultant vertical force acts at x = (MR − MO)/W = (648 − 216)/432 = 1.0 m from the toe. The eccentricity from the centre is e = 1.5 − 1.0 = 0.5 m, which equals B/6 = 0.5 m, so the resultant lies exactly at the edge of the middle third. Base pressures q = (W/B)(1 ± 6e/B) = 144(1 ± 1): toe 288 kPa, heel 0 kPa. The whole base is just in contact, and the toe pressure must be checked against the bearing resistance.

(f) Above the water table (0–3 m): σ'a at 3 m = ⅓ × 18 × 3 = 18 kPa. Below it, σ'v at 6 m = 54 + 3 × (20 − 9.81) = 84.6 kPa, so σ'a = 28.2 kPa. The soil thrust comes in three parts: triangle 0–3 m = ½ × 18 × 3 = 27.0 kN/m; rectangle 3–6 m = 18 × 3 = 54.0 kN/m; triangle 3–6 m = ½ × 10.2 × 3 = 15.3 kN/m. Total soil thrust = 96.3 kN/m. Water pressure at the base = 9.81 × 3 = 29.4 kPa, giving a water thrust of ½ × 29.4 × 3 = 44.1 kN/m. Total horizontal thrust = 140.4 kN/m.

Comment: although the effective soil thrust drops (because the submerged soil is lighter), the water acts with K = 1, so the total thrust rises by about 30%. Moments about the base: 27 × 4 + 54 × 1.5 + 15.3 × 1 + 44.1 × 1 = 248 kNm/m, so the overturning FoS falls to 648/248 ≈ 2.6. The sliding FoS also falls; uplift under the base, which this simple calculation ignores, would make it worse still. Keeping the drains working is therefore essential. In practice these checks would be made with Eurocode 7 partial factors (BS EN 1997-1 Design Approach 1) rather than lumped factors of safety.

questions.q: A developer plans a four-storey residential block with a basement on a former industrial site in outer London. The BGS map shows river terrace gravels over London Clay, and historical maps show a filled pond and a works building on the site. Discuss how you would plan the ground investigation, identifying the main geotechnical hazards and explaining what each stage and test is for.
markScheme: Starts with a desk study (BGS maps and borehole records, historical OS maps, flood and groundwater data, utilities) and a walkover, producing a preliminary ground model and hazard register

Identifies hazards: made ground or filled pond (variable, compressible, possibly contaminated, obstructions); groundwater in the terrace gravels (basement seepage, base stability); shrinkable high-plasticity London Clay (trees, heave on basement unloading); sulfates attacking concrete

Proposes phased fieldwork: trial pits to define made ground and foundations of the old works; cable percussion boreholes through the gravels into London Clay, deep enough below basement and foundation level
Specifies in-situ testing and sampling: SPTs in the gravels; tube samples in the clay; groundwater monitoring with standpipes or piezometers
Specifies laboratory testing: classification (w, Atterberg limits, PSD), undrained and drained strength (triaxial), oedometer for heave and settlement, chemical tests for contamination and sulfate
Links results to design: basement retaining wall type, groundwater control, foundation choice (e.g. piles through fill into London Clay), heave
Concludes with a ground model, interpretative report and risk register, referring to BS 5930 / BS EN 1997-2
Clear structure and justified choices
questions.modelAnswer:
The investigation should be phased, with each stage aimed at the hazards the previous stage identifies, following BS 5930 and BS EN 1997-2.

Desk study and walkover. BGS maps and nearby borehole records indicate river terrace gravels over London Clay, and give a first estimate of their thicknesses and the groundwater level in the gravels. A sequence of historical Ordnance Survey maps would locate the filled pond and the footprint of the works building, and show what the works produced, which points to possible contaminants. Flood maps, utility records and any earlier site reports complete the picture. A walkover checks access, nearby trees and the condition of neighbouring buildings. The output is a preliminary ground model and a hazard register.

Hazards. (1) Made ground, especially the infilled pond: variable, compressible and possibly containing organic material, voids, old foundations and contamination. (2) Groundwater in the permeable terrace gravels: it will flow into the basement excavation and could cause instability at its base. (3) London Clay: a high-plasticity, overconsolidated clay that shrinks and swells with moisture change, especially near trees, and that will heave when unloaded by the basement excavation. (4) Sulfates in the clay or fill, which attack buried concrete.

Fieldwork. Machine-dug trial pits would define the extent and nature of the made ground and expose old foundations and obstructions. Cable percussion boreholes would be drilled through the fill and gravels well into the London Clay, going below basement level and below the likely founding depth of piles, since piles through the fill into the clay are a probable solution. SPTs in the gravels would indicate their density. Thin-walled tube samples would be taken in the clay. Standpipes or piezometers would record groundwater levels over time, including seasonal changes. Samples of the fill and soil would be taken for chemical testing.

Laboratory testing. Water content, Atterberg limits and particle size distributions would classify the soils and indicate shrink–swell potential. Triaxial tests would give undrained and drained strength. Oedometer tests would give compressibility, for settlement and heave. Chemical tests would cover sulfate, pH and contaminants.

Use of results. The data would inform the type of basement wall (for example an embedded bored pile wall cutting off water in the gravels), the groundwater control during excavation, the foundation design and the allowance for heave. They would also determine whether any contamination needs remediation. The findings would be written up as a factual report and an interpretative report with an updated ground model and risk register. Supplementary investigation would follow if the results reveal unexpected conditions, such as a deeper pond infill.
